thesis.question: How does a shopper's cart become an order, and what keeps the systems that hold the order, its money and its books in agreement afterwards?
thesis.claim: A cart becomes an order once, at checkout, which asks each system that owns a fact for a final answer, writes those answers (price, tax, availability, delivery promise) into the order and creates it exactly once; afterwards the order, its money and its books stay in agreement only under four rules: the order has one home with three status lines (money, goods per shipment, returns), moved only by messages from the systems that witnessed each payment, shipment or return; every message and request about the order carries a business key that makes a repeat harmless, and whatever is still unresolved is checked with its source on a schedule; every action that moves money or issues a legal document has one writing system; and invoices, payout reports and bank lines are matched line by line every month on identifiers the order passes along.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the order is the shop platform's record with one status, that the thank-you page, the payment connector and the ERP connector between them keep the order, the money and the books in agreement, and that a disagreement is fixed by a better connector, a second payment provider or an order management system.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's Three-Status Order (#1052877: 'Delivered', 'In picking' and 'Not invoiced' for six days, 11 support tickets) and its Double Refund (212 returns, €19,400 refunded twice) were not faults inside any one product: each was a missing status line, writer, key or comparison. A merchant that accepts the claim writes down the order's home, the writer and the key of each money action and the monthly match before it buys an order management system or adds a payment provider.
thesis.how_why: From the moment the shopper leaves for her bank's app, the merchant's own systems no longer witness what happens: the payment provider knows whether money moved, the warehouse which lines left, the carrier which parcel arrived, and each reports by message, which can be late, out of order, repeated or lost. One status word lets the latest message overwrite the others; a request without a business key cannot be told from a retry, so a second writer or one retry moves money twice; and an invoice, which must be numbered consecutively and never edited, can come from only one system. A payout nets payments, refunds and fees from different days, so only a line-by-line match on shared identifiers shows that nothing was lost.

supporting_claims.claim: Checkout owns none of the facts it writes into the order: it asks each owning system for a final answer at the moment of commitment, so an answer taken from an out-of-date copy becomes an error that every later system inherits.

After checkout the order's systems learn what happened from messages sent by the systems that witnessed it (the payment provider, the warehouse, the carrier), which arrive late, out of order, twice or not at all; every message and request therefore carries a business key that makes a repeat harmless, and a scheduled job asks the source about everything still unresolved.
Every action that moves money or issues a legal document has exactly one writing system: one system may refund, one may capture, and one system per legal entity issues invoices and credit notes.

An order is one record with three status lines (money, goods per shipment, returns) from which the status the customer sees is computed, and once orders are created and fulfilled in several places one system must hold that record as the order's home.

Tax is computed from facts the shop owns (ship-to address, product tax category, buyer status) under rates kept once for every channel, and the invoice is issued per shipment at dispatch, never edited and corrected only by a credit note that references it.

The ledger is posted from documents and payout reports, not from payment events, and the books agree with the shop only when invoices, payout reports and bank lines are matched line by line on shared identifiers.

flow.rationale: The page opens on one Kestrel & Pine order that is paid but still reads unpaid, to which the closing returns, and narrows: from why it happens (after the click on 'pay' the facts arrive as messages from other systems, and the order reads unpaid until the PSP's message arrives), to the part's four rules and the system that handles each, with the relay and the shape figures beside the rules they picture, to Eva's one order on which the rules work, in contrast to the opening order, to one paragraph per chapter, each opening on one of the company's failures; it ends on the explained opening order and where to start. The messages come before the rules because each rule answers a property of the messages (late, repeated, from several systems); the rules come before Eva's order because her order shows the four systems at work in time; the chapter list follows Eva's order because each chapter takes one of its systems. A separate paragraph on the company's other failures was cut: readers found it out of place after Eva's order (round 3) and between the opening scene and its cause (round 4), and each chapter paragraph already names its own case. Put the rules first and they answer a problem the reader has not been shown; put the advice first and it points at chapters the reader has not met.

hook.content: A shopper pays, but the order still appears unpaid because the confirmation has not reached the shop; the warehouse cannot tell whether to dispatch it, and support cannot give a clear answer.

bridge.to_topic: The merchant's side, where checkout writes those facts into an order once and every later fact (paid, dispatched, delivered) arrives as a message from another system; and Eva's €235 order #1072455, created at 21:14 on 13 April 2027 with its payment pending, confirmed seconds later, invoiced on 14 April and reconciled at the May close.

thesis_statement.text: After checkout the facts about an order arrive as messages that may be late, out of order or repeated, so the part sets rules, one chapter for each of the order's four owners: checkout creates the order once despite retries; every message carries a key so a repeat changes nothing, and each action that moves money has one writing system; the order record keeps separate states for money, shipments and returns; and invoices, payouts and the bank are matched every month.

promises.promise: Four chapters, one for each of the order's four owners in the sequence the order meets them: checkout creating the order once despite retries; the payment provider, with a key on every message and one writing system for each action that moves money; the order record with separate states for money, shipments and returns; the ledger, with the monthly match of invoices, payouts and the bank.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At Kestrel & Pine, the fictional outdoor brand, a shopper can have paid while the shop still shows the order unpaid, so the warehouse cannot tell whether to dispatch and support cannot answer.

evidence.what: A paid order that reads unpaid because the confirmation has not reached the shop; a warehouse that cannot decide; support with no clear answer.
evidence.shows: Three people who need the same fact about one order and cannot get it from the shop's own record.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Once the shopper clicks 'pay' and checkout creates the order, the shop learns what happened only from messages (the payment service provider's webhook, the warehouse's dispatch, the carrier's delivery) that may arrive late, out of order or twice; until the PSP's message arrives, the order reads unpaid.

evidence.what: The PSP glossed as the system that handles the money and reports through a webhook (a server-to-server notification); the warehouse reports dispatch, the carrier delivery.
evidence.shows: Why the shop can be the last to know: the facts are witnessed elsewhere and reach it by message.

sections.heading: Chapters in this part
sections.controlling_idea: Each of the four chapters decides one question about the order and opens on one Kestrel & Pine case, and each starts where the one before handed the order on.

advances_thesis.how: Each paragraph introduces the chapter that argues one or more of the part's supporting claims, so the list is the part's argument in outline.

flow.rationale: Each chapter starts where the one before it handed the order on and uses what that chapter fixed. Checkout comes first because it creates the order with its payment pending and introduces the webhook and the key on order creation; the payments chapter follows that pending payment through its four stages and makes the key and the single writer the rule for every action that moves money; the order chapter needs the money status line the payments chapter defined and adds the goods line per shipment, the returns line and split shipments; the ledger chapter comes last because it invoices per shipment, which needs split shipments, and matches payout reports, which need the payments chapter's stages. Putting payments first would explain a webhook for an order the reader has not seen created; putting the order chapter before payments would name a money status line before the reader knows what moves it; putting the ledger before the order chapter would ask for one invoice per shipment before the reader knows that an order can leave in two parcels.

transition_in.carries_over: The four rules and the company whose failures open the chapters.
transition_in.introduces: One paragraph per chapter: the question in bold, the case it opens on and what the chapter does about it.

conclusion.so_what: The reader knows the opening order is settled by a rule (the provider's message marks it paid), not by the thank-you page, and starts where the order is created.

callback.how: The reader can now say what marks it paid.

transition_in.introduces: What they explain together about the opening's order, and where to begin.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The opening's unpaid order is now explained (the provider's message, not the thank-you page, marks it paid); begin with the checkout chapter.
